Did I understand the hon.
member to say that the goods were not unloaded at all at Miquelon?

subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext:
Oh, yes, of course they
are unloaded. But why did the leader of the opposition make reference to Miquelon? He was right in his reference. But it was not complete. I am now endeavouring to show what it means. For what purpose was Mi-

Export Act-Mr. Bourassa

quelon brought in? Why was a reference made to the million dollars' worth of whisky shipped there? Why was that done, if the leader of the opposition did not foresee the consequences of this legislation as applied to goods destined for the United States but interrupted for a few days at Miquelon just for the purpose of evading the American law and now our own law as well? Of course our tribunals may put a different construction upon this legislation; but I am not speaking on the legal aspect of the question at the moment; I am dealing with the international question. I am not acquainted with the secrets of the government, nor do I know what is in the mind of the leader of the opposition, but If the object of this bill is sincerely and earnestly to prevent Canadian whisky from going to the United States, I venture the prediction that it will not prevent the exportation of the one-hundredth part of what is being exported at the present time. The profits of the distiller and of the bootleggers will be diminished, because instead of going straight across to the United States, cynically, but with less hypocrisy, now they will go the round-about way. It may curtail their profits, but I can assure you that there will be plenty of it left.
This morning I came down from Toronto; perhaps it is because I have been in Toronto that what remains of my puritanism has been shaken up, but on the way I picked up the Globe and the Mail. I am very impartial as between the two papers and two parties. In one of those newspapers I read of a lawsuit which has been commenced by the American government against a millionaire bootlegger in Chicago or elsewhere. They had such precise information with regard to him that they were suing for nearly $1,000,000 in income tax, all from profits derived from the importation of liquor into the United States. If one man has made such profits that the American government claim nearly $1,000,000 in income tax for three or four years, do you think there will not remain enough profit to enable these people to evade our laws and to laugh at us as they are laughing now at the American government?
I am glad the hon. member for Nelson made this point; the leader of the opposition referred to it also, but happy and witty as he was I do not think he took the possible consequences seriously enough. What is the use of concealing the truth? A nation of 10,000,000 people, with no other neighbour on the continent, is not capable of playing with a nation of 120,000,000 people, as big nations generally play with small nations. Follow the trend of diplomacy, whether it is American,

French, German or English; look at the difference in tone between a despatch sent by a big power to a small power, and the answer of a small nation to a large nation. That aspect of the situation is serious, and it is far better that we should admit it. I know it is hard for the Prime Minister to admit that situation, but I think it would be far better if he did so. The older I grow the more I grow tired of shams and round-about methods of concealing the truth. It may be that the request for this legislation was made in a polite manner, but no doubt it was made firmly; and we know what that means under the hands of statesmen who have at their backs the wealth and the military force, or if you like the economic force, of the United States. From the international point of view, that would be the only reason which would justify us in passing this law.
Supposing British Guiana asked us to pass a law similar to this; do you think for a moment we would even consider doing so? Of course we would not. Even if a country like France or Italy asked us to do so we would refuse, and rightly so. Therefore if we do it because it is the American government, or because of our close neighbourhood, or because of the power of the American government to make good their claims upon us, then let us face the consequences like men. I am quite sure that the pressure which has been brought to bear in order to secure this legislation has been "friendly"; but we may be sure that as time goes on the pressure will be perhaps a little less friendly and a little more pressing when it is found that this legislation is inoperative.
The government, I presume, have a knowledge of the responsibilities which will be entailed by this legislation. I do not ask that the government tell us everything they know; I am not so unreasonable. I think at times all governments conceal too many things, but there are occasions when a government, in the accomplishment of its duty to the state, cannot tell everything, but in such a case it is better to say nothing. A government may say just enough to raise suspicion, to create doubts and bring about apprehension; and we in parliament and the people outside ask, "What is it? what is the danger? to what degree does it extend?" What will be the end of the exigencies of the American government in this matter? We do not know, and I am sure the government does not know. Perhaps even the American government does not know, because like us they are subject to currents and counter-currents of opinion. If as is expected by all reasonable men, the movement

Export Act-Mr. Adshead
against prohibition gains ground; if the unholy alliance between the prohibitionists, the bootleggers and the moonshiners is finally broken up by the common sense and the morality of the American people, what will be the situation? I may say in parentheses that I believe that in the United States, with all their faults, there is still an enormous reserve of common sense and true morality; but, as in other democratic countries, that common sense and morality have not always a chance to reach public bodies and to control electorates. However, if the true sentiment of the United States, what I call common 'sense and reason, prevails and breaks up that unholy alliance between what we might call the powers of good and the powers of evil, then we may rest quiet, and four or five years hence we will hear no more of this legislation than we will hear of the Volstead Act itself. If on the other hand the American nation, willingly or unwillingly, decide to maintain this law and to exercise their unlimited strength, political, social and economic, in having their own law applied, and in praying us first, and gradually forcing us, to apply our own law passed at their behest in order to maintain good relations, then I say we should take this action with open eyes and piepare to do much more than is apparent at the moment. We must prepare to stand by the consequences of our actions, one of which is, that if we want to preserve the friendship of the United States by making this law good, we must be ready to solve a few difficult questions which may arise with France, for example, and perhaps with other countries as well. The process which is going on at Miquelon is also going on, to a lesser degree, in the Dutch Indies. I have just returned from a tour of that part of the world, and I can assure hon. gentlemen that what the American government is complaining about so far as Canada is concerned, is taking place in almost every one of the West Indies, French, British, Dutch, and negro, and what is not unloaded at Miquelon will be carried by Canadian National Steamship boats to Nassau, to St. Lucia, to Barbados, to Bermuda, and to Jamaica, and will then find its way back to its final destination, the United States, the most virtuous, perhaps, but certainly the most thirsty nation upon the face of the earth.
We know something about this in Quebec. When the puritans of the other provinces lift their hands in horror at the amount of whisky consumed in the province of Quebec, they should know, first, that nine-tenths of that whisky is made in Ontario and Scotland, and that two-thirds of it is consumed by the
puritans and the prohibitionists from the United States. In the old days the sanctimonious prohibitionists of Ontario were also responsible for a share. But now, thank heaven, the people of Ontario drink their share in their own province, we drink our share in our province, and all the trouble with excess drinking is found to be between the months of June and September, when the tourists, full of enthusiasm for the beautiful scenery of Canada, come to admire the Laurentian mountains and the majestic waters of the St. Lawrence but nevertheless, and quite rightly, decide that the waters of the St. Lawrence do not make a proper beverage. Before going down to Quebec to admire the old citadel and to see the beauties of the Saguenay, they consume a full and ample share of the liquid distilled in Ontario and sold by the agents of the Quebec government.
Let us face the truth, Mr. Chairman, as nothing is gained by hypocrisy. Rightly or wrongly, Canada has brought about a great improvement in the government control of the making and sale of liquor. This great United States has undertaken to prohibit the making and consumption of liquor but has not succeeded in bringing the whole of its
120,000,000 people in line with its law, and I do not think that Canada is capable of making that nation more dry and law abiding than is the American government itself.
I leave these remarks to the reflection o. the government and of the opposition; because in a matter like this, apart from certain propositions held both by the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition, I think it was a great object lesson that the leaders of both parties did not make a party issue of this international affair. They could however have spared themselves the moral portion of their orations; because when two unmarried gentlemen decide to live together and commune on moral issues, I am tempted to say, with the old Latin jurists: "Connubium contra naturam".

subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think
the other portion of Alberta should be heard from. I have listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) with considerable interest, and he seems to have based his whole argument upon the theory that Canada would be responsible for liquor shipments after they had left Canada and reached some other port not within the boundaries of Canada, which shipments might find their way to the United States after a second clearance had been obtained. I cannot

Export Act-Mr. Adshead

agree with that argument, and I do not think the government agrees with it. I would like to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) answer that point. I do not think the members of the opposition who have spoken upon this question entertain that idea at all.
Although the bill reads, "destined for delivery" it is only intended that clearances shall be refused to vessels carrying liquor to the United States. If the liquor is destined for France, whether it be the ports of St. Pierre and Miquelon, or the port of Paris, both places being upon French territory and under the same laws, it could not fee held that Canada would be responsible for such liquor finding its way to the United States under a second clearance. That would seem to be an utterly absurd argument, but the remarks of those opposed to this bill seem to be based upon that supposition.
The hon. member for Labelle stated that he was going to vote for this bill, and yet he speaks with a'lfl his heart and soul against it

 there did not seem to be one thing in the bill which he approved of. This is my fourth year in this House of Commons and I am sorry to say that I am beginning to become rather cynical. I do not know whether it is because I am not trusting my fellow members as much as I should, but it seems that every time a bill is brought uip the sincerity of the mover, the sincerity of the government or the sincerity of the opposition is called into question. I was discussing this question to-day with a few members at the luncheon table, and they seemed to be in doubt as to the object of the government in introducing this bill. They said, "Is it a moral question, is it because it is^ right?" "Oh, no, that could not be." "Why is it introduced, do they hope to obtain the votes of the women of Canada?" Those votes are not sufficient to affect an election, and we could not find any real reason for the ini reduction of this bill unless it were the motives suggested by the right hon. the Prime Minister in his opening address. I would seem to be confirmed in that view by the opening remarks of the leader of the opposition, who said:
I shall endeavour-and it will take some little time-to strip from the right hon. gentleman that mantle of assumed virtue that he has worn to-day.
We have the leader of the opposition attributing to the Prime Minister of Canada a mantle of assumed virtue, which mantle he proceeded to strip from around the shoulders of the right hon. the Prime Minister, only to
f\Ir. Adshead.]
wrap it about himself. The one takes it from the other.
I am going to support this bill in an effort to strip myself of any cynicism which I have. Whatever may be the motives of the Prime Minister in introducing this bill, I quite agree with the hon. members for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) a,nd Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) when they said that it would remove a certain stigma from the name of Canada, caused by cooperation with the bootlegger. We are making it clear that Canada does not intend to go hand in hand with bootleggers and rum runners.
It has been suggested by hon. members that this measure has been brought forward' at the instigation of the United States, and that, therefore, the present Liberal government is acting under the influence and dictation of the American government. Similar things have been said in reference to tariff measures, and I must protest that when we cannot agree on certain principles the activity of hon. members should not be expended in endeavouring to show that such things are done at the dictation of the United States. Surely we can be Canadians together and surely we can discuss these measures upon their merits as they concern Canada instead of saying that our opponents are taking the stand they do at the dictation of the United States. These things make a new member, one who has not been very long in the house, feel cynical so that whatever the other hon. gentleman is going to say about this matter, we wonder, when he attributes these motives, whether there is any sincerity in the whole business or not.
A good deal has been said about the money loss. So far as I know the liquor traffic, the loss of revenue received from it is far outbalanced by the removal of the consequences of the traffic itself. While I am not an entire prohibitionist, I believe that revenue received from that source is never a credit to any country or any government, and if there is a loss, while it may be a revenue loss, it will be far more than made up by gains in. other directions.
The point raised by the hon. member for Fort William was, I think, well taken, namely, that we might better have had a treaty. In fact, an hon. member drew my attention to a statement, reported at page 621 of Hansard of what Mr. Phillips said when addressing the Prime Minister. He said:
While the government of the United States appreciates the gracious offer of the Canadian government to permit American officials to transmit information of this kind from Canadian soil, it remains convinced that the only effective means of dealing with the smuggling

Export Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
problem along the border is the conclusion of a treaty amending the convention of June 6, 1924, to the end that clearance be denied to shipments of commodities from either country when their importation is prohibited in the other.
Mr. Phillips expresses the wish that the government make a treaty. I suppose such a treaty would not have been one-sided ; that we would have had a quid pro quo. Mr. Phillips does not in that statement refer specifically to liquor; he refers to any article which may be prohibited from entering one country or the other. I should like to hear from the Prime Minister in that regard whether the United States is prepared to offer a prohibition of any commodity which Canada might not wish to return for the prohibition which we are giving to them in the matter of liquor clearances.
The bill, however, goes a little further. It says "any country," so that it does not apply specifically to the United States. The bill would apply to Argentina, France, Germany, any other country, and while the point made by the hon. member for St. Lawrenoe-St. George this afternoon did' not.strike me very forcibly when I noted it down, after I heard it elaborated, it did, namely, that liquor is at the present time a legal commodity in Canada. Last year the Minister of National Revenue stated the same thing very forcibly; he said that alcoholic liquor was just as much a legal commodity in Canada as cotton .or anything else. Therefore, it was pointed out by my hon. friend, we were virtually saying that if any country asked us to prohibit the entry into it of any commodity that was legal in Canada, this same measure would apply. I think the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George specifically mentioned matches as a commodity which could not be given clearance for export to France if France asked that they should not be exported, because they are prohibited from import into that country. That point might very well be explained by the government in answering criticisms that have been made in regard to this legislation. I do not wish to delay the committee any longer. I am in favour of this measure; perhaps for once I believe the government is sincere in bringing it forward and^ I will do my utmost to make it a success.

speechtext: How many countries in the world have prohibition in regard to which this bill would apply? If it applies only to the United States, why was that particular country not mentioned instead of the matter being put in a general way?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext:
I am afraid 1 cannot tell my hon. friend how many countries
there are. The bill is drafted in relation to our own officials and it is for the purpose of controlling the actions of our own officials with respect to the exporting of liquor to a country the laws of which it is known prohibit its importation. If their actions should be controlled at all as regards one country prohibiting liquor importations they ought equally to be controlled in that regard toward any other country having a like prohibition. I think that is the reason why the term "any country" is used.
May I say I. have not spoken thus far because I do not wish to delay the passage o: my own measure. I assume, however, hon. gentlemen will expect me to say a word with regard to some of the points which they have raised. I hardly expected that the measure would meet with the full approval of hon. gentlemen opposite. What was most significant in the remarks of those immediately opposite who spoke is the fact that while they all purported to support the principle of the bill, in the speeches they made they were all against the bill itself. As regards the remarks of hon. gentlemen immediately opposite, I think I am correct in saying that they were for the most part either aimed at a postponement of the measure or were critical of its being legislation concerned with a matter of domestic interest to the United States rather than one of immediate concern to our own country. In that particular may I say that I believe much of the criticism has arisen from hon. members not realizing that this is a purely Canadian measure, related exclusively to work of administration by Canadian officials? It is not a measure for the enforcement of prohibition in the United States or which, except as to its possible consequences, has anything to do with the enforcement of any laws of the United States as they exist at the present time. It has to do with our own business and our own affairs, and it is intended entirely and exclusively for that purpose. It is not a measure to prohibit the importation of liquor into the United States under all circumstances and in every way. That is wherein several hon. members who have spoken to-day have entirely misjudged the measure, whether intentionally or not I cannot say. It is a measure to control our own affairs and our own officials, the aim being to prevent officials of the government in the exercise of their official duties from cooperating immediately and directly with rum runners and bootleggers. That is what the measure is for and for nothing more than that.
I might repeat in a word what I said the other day. This measure prevents officials of

Export Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
the government from releasing liquor which is known by them to be destined to a country that prohibits its importation, liquor which is declared in the export entry to be so destined.

subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext: My hon. friend has made his speech; will he let me make mine? In the second place, it seeks to prevent officials from granting permits over their own signatures as officials of the Dominion government for the removal of liquor from distilleries for export into a country which prohibits its importation, permits which in their effect simply enable the liquor to get from a distillery into the hands of criminal gangs and rum runners. That control is all within Canada; not the least part of it up to that point has to do with liquor actually crossing the border. It is simply controlling the actions of our officials who, it is alleged, for the purpose of collecting revenue, sign these permits, which permits when signed have the effect in fact of linking the Dominion government in a way with rum runners in their operations of smuggling liquor into a country which prohibits its importation.

subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext: May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext: My hon. friend has made his speech. I think he should let me make mine.

subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext:
Are the criminals to whom
the Prime Minister refers criminals under the laws of Canada? The rum runners to whom he refers are a single dozen of them Canadian citizens, who are subject to our own law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext:
No, these rum runners I believe are for the most part American citizens. If we are going to cooperate with American citizens, let us cooperate with the respectable element in the United States, and not with the rum runners and bootleggers. The whole purpose of this measure is to lend the control of government, so far as the government has control in this matter, to those elements in this country and in other countries that are seeking to uphold the enforcement of law, and not to permit the officials of this country to become the instruments whereby the work of rum runners and bootleggers wifi be facilitated. That is the whole purpose of the bill. If my hon. friend will believe the wording of the law as it is, 
and not try to make out that it is something that it is not; if he will just look at it as it is drafted and see what it purports to be, he will discover that what I am saying is absolutely correct. This law relates to the officials of the government of Canada, and only to the officials of the government of Canada. It may have as a consequence the prevention of the exportation of liquor into the United States and into any other country which prohibits the importation of liquor, but its primary purpose is to see that so far as this country is concerned, we as a country and this government as a government and its officials do not become parties in any particular to facilitating the nefarious operations of those persons who for purposes of personal gain are engaged in the business of violating the laws of another country. That is the purpose, and as such I would think that it must command the unanimous support of the entire house and of parliament.
Some effort has been made to interpret, or rather should I say, to misinterpret, Dord Curzons remarks, and my own application of them to the possible serious consequences that may come at any moment if present conditions are permitted to continue. May I explain exactly what was in my own mind in what I have said? Hon. members must have noticed a little while ago how quickly feeling was aroused in .this country by the sinking on the high seas of one rum running vessel which was pursued by an American vessel and ultimately sunk with the loss of one life. The person who lost his life did not happen to be a Canadian, but a citizen of some other country.

subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext: He was a Frenchman.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext:
Hon. members saw how feeling in the country to the south as well as in our own country was aroused over that single incident, an incident which having regard to all the circumstances, but for principles of international law involved, had few if any features to commend it to the attention of anybody. Let us assume, instead of a happening of that kind on the high seas, that to-morrow between Windsor and Detroit, [DOT]as a result of some official action hastily taken in connection with this rum running business, a vessel were to be sunk and a dozen lives lost, six of those lost being Canadians and six Americans, and it were shown that as respects the liquor being smuggled into the United States aboard the vessel, as it could be shown under present conditions, the government of Canada through its own officials had released that liquor from a distil-

Export Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
lery in Canada knowing that it had been entered for export undeT a written statement made by the person who secured its release from the distillery, which statement set forth that it -was destined for the United States; and that it was shown further that the liquor was removed from the distillery to the dock on a permit issued by a government official of this country, the permit itself stating that the liquor was to be removed to the dock from which the vessel sailed for export to the United States, though all the while it was known that liquor could not be legally shipped into the United States; and further, that the liquor was cleared for the United States by officials who knew that it could not get into the United States legally, but that they were delivering it into the hands of rum runners whose purpose it was to smuggle it in illegally.
I ask my hon. friend what position would this country be in, when it came to settling an international incident of that kind.

subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext: I will answer at once. This country is in this position. Under the treaty negotiated in 1924 by your own Minister of Justice, acting on behalf of your own government, this country is in the position that the United States recognizes that it has the lawful right to send liquor out of Canadian ports by Canadian clearances direct to any American port on either the Atlantic or the Pacific. That is the clear implication of the treaty you signed yourself.

subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext: And we have been doing that for years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext: Are my hon. friends upholding the view that we should continue the practice of having our officials sign these documents?

subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN

So far as I am concerned I view with the utmost astonishment the fact that the Prime Minister in the face of the resolutions of this parliament and the findings of his own commission has continued these conditions down to this day, and I am astonished at the further fact that when invited to make a convention with the United States, which would be equitable and which would be reciprocal for both countries, the Prime Minister refused to enter into those negotiations.

In a hurried

Hurrying

Export Act-Mr. Mackenzie King

The point I
wish to make clear is this: It is impossible for the government in any legislation of this kind to hope to please my hon. friend and those who think like him. We cannot hope to bring down legislation that is going to meet his wishes when he tells us in one and the same breath that the legislation we bring down goes too far and does not go far enough, that it does not do enough in the way of enforcement while at the same time it does too much in the way of enforcement.

subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN

The legislation, my hon. friend says, ought to have been brought down years ago, and now that it is being brought down he says it is being brought down in too much of a hurry.
Hon. gentlemen opposite complain that we did not proceed by way of a treaty. What would have been the criticism we would have heard from them if we had come into this parliament with a treaty made with the United States at this time?

subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext: It would have been far better for Canada than what you are putting through now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext: We know what the criticism of hon, gentlemen opposite would have been: It would have been that we had gone out of our way in order to go to Washington again to make a treaty. That is what we would have heard from them. May I tell my hon. friends apposite exactly the position we are in? If they have read the despatches carefully they will notice that at the time of the conference the government directed attention to the fact that the Americans were stressing the need for a treaty dealing only with one thing, namely liquor.; and that we stressed the desire of dealing with merchandise generally.

subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext: And they consented to it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext:
Exactly. And having consented to it, I imagine they will now be prepared to carry out any undertaking they were ready to carry ouit then. So we 
are in (this happy position to-day: We have hon. gentlemen apposite and their press joining with us in the view that we ought to have a treaty. May I tell them, so that their minds will be relieved immediately, that having cleaned our own skirts so far as the actions of our own officials are concerned, we are proceeding now to get a treaty, and we will see to it that it is broad enough to cover all articles of merchandise. We are in a strong position, we are able to assure our neighbours that on this we are all of one mind. I hope that hon. gentlemen opposite, when the treaty is presented to this house, as I hope it will be shortly, will gave us their unanimous approval of it.

It has been suggested that we take the first part of section one.
Notwithstanding the provisions of any other statute or law or of any regulation made thereunder or of any bond, agreement or other instrument relating thereto.

subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext:
Before that is put, I would like to make a few observations in connection with this bill. In the first place, we have heard nothing from the government as to why they have changed their policy of less than a year ago. That policy was applauded by all the members on the government side of the house, and by a goodly portion of both the press of Canada and the United States. It is my submission that the house is entitled to that information, because one department of the government of the great country to the south of us has practically acknowledged its failure to enforce the Volstead Act, and is now passing the buck by laying the blame on Canada, although only from 2 to 4 per cent of the liquor consume! in the United States is exported from this country. At the present time the Volstead Act is a national joke across the border, and they would now swear in the Canadian government as part of their police force to help enforce this American law. The eighteenth amendment is a political issue in the United States, and that being the case I think it would be well for us to wait a while, and see how they come out with the poll which is being taken by the Literary Digest, and which is showing distinctly that the majority of the people on the other side of the line are opposed to the eighteenth amendment.

89r,
Export Act-Mr. Robinson
I find fault with the proposed legislation for the reason that in my opinion it would be hard to convince the -people of this country that the United States is not interfering with our domestic and internal affairs. That condition is borne out by the fact that the United States government within the last few months sent a delegation to this country demanding, practically, that we should cut off clearances to that country. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Oahan) supports me in that by the statement he made this afternoon to the effect that a prominent official of that country had practically demanded that we would have to meet their wishes in that respect.
In May last, according to the Border Cities Star, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated that Canada had gone about as far as it could go, and that the United States was not trying to cooperate with us, or was not taking advantage of our assistance in helping it to carry out its law. May I read what the Border Cities Star has to say in this regard in its publication of May 16, 1929:
The Dominion government has absolutely refused the request of the United States that clearances of liquor laden ships bound from Windsor and other points on the Detroit river and the great lakes for Detroit and other United States ports be refused. The Canadian government believes it would not be warranted in such action because Canadian sentiment would not support prohibition of the export of liquor even to a country in which alcoholic beverages may not legally be imported.
There has been considerable publicity in regard to the city of Windsor, which happens to be in my riding. One would think that we had export docks from one end of the city to the other; the fact is that we have only two. This is the letter dated May 16, 1929, from the Secretatry of State for External Affairs, Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, to the charge d'affaires of the United States legation. It is as follows:
Referring to your note number 272 of the 27th November, 1928. and to the discussion which took place at the conference of officials on the subject of commercial smuggling held in Ottawa on the 7th-10th of January, 1929, I now have the honour to state that the Canadian government has given consideration to all aspects of the existing situation, and has examined the report of the Canadian representatives to the conference, a copy of which is herewith enclosed for the information of your government.	_
As you will observe from an examination of the report, the conference devoted its attention almost exclusively to discussion of the suggestion made by the United States representatives that the Canadian government, in addition to the numerous steps already taken, which facilitate the enforcement of the United States laws
against the importation of liquor and which are summarized in the report, should prohibit the export of intoxicating liquors to the United States.
Without making at the present time a final decision on this proposal, the Canadian government is in accord with the opinion expressed by the Canadian representatives that the problem of enforcement facing United States officials, particularly in Detroit and Niagara border, might in large measure be solved by a further extension of the system^ of furnishing information as to shipments of liquor provided by the convention of June, 1924.
It will be noted from the report that instructions hate been issued to Canadian customs officials to provide more detailed and exact information as to shipments, and that more recently steps have been taken to reduce the number of export docks, which will facilitate securing more complete and accurate data. To cooperate with and assist further the government of the United States in the effective enforcement of its laws, the Canadian government is prepared to permit United States officers to be stationed on the Canadian side of the border, at ports of clearance to be determined. in order to enable the United States officials themselves to transmit immediately to the appropriate authorities in the United States information to be furnished by the Canadian customs officials as clearances are obtained as to the clearance of all vessels for the United States carrying liquor cargoes.
Any further suggestions which would make for increased speed, accuracy, or precision in the conveyance of information to the appropriate United States officials will be sympathetically considered.
Accept, sir, the renewed assurances of my highest consideration.
W. L. Mackenzie King,
Secretary of State for External Affairs.
In answer to that statement we find the following in the columns of the Philadelphia Ledger, a very prominent journal of the United States:
Canada's courteous but firm refusal to take the steps asked by the United States to curb border rum running prevented the antismuggling conference at Ottawa from getting anywhere. The chief proposal rejected was that the Dominion seek to prohibit the exportation of liquor to the United States by refusing clearance to vessels bound to this country with cargoes of alcoholic beverages.
This attitude of Canadian officials is perfectly clear. Their position is that the suggested export restrictions might make every cove along that country's extended coast line a harbour for rum smugglers, entailing heavy expense for enforcement to hold up the Dominion's end of the bargain. Public sentiment is also a factor, for only two of the provinces now favour prohibition.
In view of these considerations, there is nothing unfriendly in the Canadian query as to why the United States could not strengthen her own laws to handle the problem instead of appealing to another country for assistance.
The Dominion has taken certain steps to aid in curbing smuggling, and undoubtedly feels she has gone as far as she can in this direction.
89C
Export Act-Mr. Robinson

After all, this is a problem for the United States to solve, if possible. While further aid from Canada would be helpful, that country cannot reasonably be asked to do more at the cost of undue sacrifice.
Here is a letter from Representative F. H. LaGuardia, Republican of New York state:
Washington, June 4. "Dry" America consumes more Canadian liquor than does "wet" Canada, Representative F. H. LaGuardia (R) of New York declared in the house. He lauded Canada's refusal to make a treaty with the United States forbidding exportation of liquor to this country.
"Canada has done more in helping enforcement of the prohibition laws in the United States than the government of the United States has been able to do," said LaGuardia; continuing:
"The present demands made on the Canadian government are nothing but a confession of weakness on the part of the United States government and an example of the complete failure of prohibition.
"Yet the government of the United States has the audacity to ask the foreign country to do that which apparently it has been unable to do within its own borders."
We might have sympathy with the United States government in the enforcement of their prohibition laws, but it is apparent to every fair-minded person that they are making only a haphazard attempt to enforce the law, and I think I can prove this fairly well later on. They say there are six carloads of liquor going into the city of Washington every month, coming from Canada, although of course I do not know how it gets through. During the past winter the Detroit News had photographs taken of the roads over the ice from the Canadian shore to the American side all along the frontier. They sent a reporter and a photographer up in an airplane, and from two o'clock in the afternoon until five o'clock in the evening they counted 75 automobiles and trucks going over the ice, loaded with beer and liquor from Amhersttmrg docks. No intelligent person can tel! me that the United States, with its army of enforcement officers on the border, could not stop that traffic. We all remember when young Laframboise was shot; the American officers did not take after the boatloads of liquor going across, but chased the chap in the car. I would say there is only a very shallow attempt being made to enforce the law, particularly along the Detroit river and the shores of lake Erie.
The Minister of National Revenue is quoted in the Border Cities Star of July 31 as follows:
Rational Revenue Chief in New Criticism of Washington
The minister drew attention to the fact that under the United States law these small liquorrunning vessels do not require to have registered 
names, but merely numbers. It was an easy matter for the operators to change the numbers, and the Canadian customs officials have no means of knowing whether the number of a vessel being cleared was the registered number.
This is the weak reply of the United States to that statement:
The Canadian authorities had asked the United States authorities if it would not be possible to secure a check-up of the registered numbers so that the vessels might be more closely identified at Canadian ports, which would permit of more authentic information being furnished the American preventive forces. The American reply to this proposal was that they "hadn't" the staff.
Then I have a letter which appeared in the Toronto Globe of February 1, which may be of interest since it was in that great moral daily:
Liquor Export Question
To the Editor of the Globe: The hon. Mr. Euler recently stated that the inland revenue tax received by the Dominion of Canada on liquor exported to the United States in the past year amounted to $13,000,000.
Just recently also the United States congress authorized the expenditure of $33,000,000 to attempt to enforce their so-called prohibition law.
From this it would appear that the United otates are only willing to spend less than 30 cents per head of its population to do this work, but. according to rumour, they are asking the people of Canada to forego a revenue on its legitimate business of at least $1.30 per head.
If the Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King really intends to ask the present session of parliament to prohibit the export of liquor to the United States, I hope he is quite sure the people of Canada, especially the thrifty people of Quebec. are so magnamimous that they are willing to have their taxes increased by $1.30 for every man, woman and child, plus several million dollars more for enforcement of such an act, at the suggestion of a country which has never done anything but try to injure Canada commercially. How the United States would jeer at us if the shoe w-as on the other foot.
I have a few articles here which are not my opinions but which contain the opinions of nationally known men in the United States as to what they think of the prohibition law. I am bringing this out in order to impress upon the house that the United States should clean up its own backyard instead of asking Canada to do it. The first article I wish to read is dated February 24, and refers to Senator George W. Norris, one of the dry leaders of the United States:
Senator George W. Norris, leading dry, chairman of the Senate judiciary committee, introduces a resolution for an investigation of the methods of prohibition enforcement and the prohibition department's personnel.
"The object of my resolution," he explains, "is to determine whether or not prohibition can be enforced. In my opinion, an honest

Export Act-Mr. Robinson
effort to enforce it has not yet been made. . . .
I admit that the problem is a very difficult one. But I feel that until the President takes the appointment of prohibition officers entirely out of politics no real effort to solve it will be made. ... I suppose it is a matter of common knowledge that, at present, the prohibition department is entirely shot through with graft and corruption. I have received within the past few weeks a quantity of evidence which shows such condition.
Then I have the opinion of Judge Paul J. McCormick, who was a member of President Hoover's crime commission and who also was a federal judge in New York where he was noted for having padlocked so many of the night clubs. This is dated Los Angeles, December 22:
Federal Judge Paul .T. McCormick, returning here after four months in the east as a member of President Hoover's national commission of law enforcement and observance, said the commission's inquiry had resulted in the conclusion that two major problems demanded immediate settlement. He named these as (1) The solution of prohibition enforcement, and (2) The removal of "governmental lawlessness" itself.
The Deputy Secretary of State for Michigan was reported in the Detroit Fress Press of December 5, as follows:
Michigan's home brew consumption averages 10 pints a month for every man, woman and child. With the end of the first rush for malt tax stamps, receipts from the new law have settled to a steady income of about $100,000 a month, according to Sidney Schulte, Deputy Secretary of State. Having completed a research into the productive qualities of a can of malt, Schulte has concluded every dollar received from the tax represents consumption of 400 pints of home made lager. In placing the average consumption at 10 pints a month Schulte estimates the state's population at
4,000,000.
The first three months of the new tax produced $400,000 but the receipts of the first month were more than double those of any month since, because dealers stocked up with stamps when the law took effect.
"And $400,000 means 100,000,000 bottles of beer." the Deputy Secretary of State slyly pointed out.
Governor Fred W. Green of the state of Michigan is quoted in an article appearing in the Detroit Free Press of October 10, as follows :
Although the files in the state department contain the names of Detroit's several hundred alley brewers, Governor Fred W. Green said to-day that this information will not be turned over to the Detroit police or federal officers unless requested. And even if it is sought by the police the governor is not certain that he would permit it to be used.
The article continues:
The names of Detroit's alley brewery operators are included in the monthly sales reports of malt manufacturers. These reports 2419-57
are submitted so that the state can enforce the new tax of 5 cents a pound and 6 cents a gallon on malt. The secretary of state's department takes it for granted that when a man buys as much as 50 barrels or more of malt a month, he is operating an alley brewery and is supplying beer to some of Detroit's thousands of blind pigs.
And again:
A publication .printed by the Malt Dealers' Association estimated recently that Detroit has 400 alley breweries which buy malt from Michigan manufacturers. Sidney A. Schulte, Deputy Secretary of State, would not reveal to-day whether his files show there are that many large buyers outside of stores.
The following article appeared in the Detroit Free Press of January 5, in connection with a suit brought in the circuit court against an insurance company for the payment of a policy upon the life of a man who had been killed in a blind pig. Apparently this blind pig was a confectionery store upon one of the main highways and it was contended that anyone who was known could obtain any kind of drink in this establishment. The article reads:
Popular acceptance of blind pigs as places of relaxation and the prevalence of drinking in all strata of society were emphasized by Circuit Judge Vincent M. Brennan Saturday when he decided that Mrs. Lulu Anders was entitled to collect $1,000 from the Title Guaranty and Casualty Company of America in indemnity for the death of her husband, killed in a blind pig hold-up.
Judge Brennan continues:
It is true that blind pig patrons occasionally are disturbed by gunmen: but so are clergymen, policemen and judges. The accepted census of blind pigs in Detroit is 15,000.
The judge continues:
Michigan became legally dry on March 1, 1918. The national prohibition act became operative January 20, 1920. After more than ten years' trial of the prohibition law in this state, the court must take judicial notice that prohibition in law is not prohibition in fact.
The time has now come when it is the duty of courts to take judicial notice that liquor is served not only in blind pigs, speak-easies. dives and spots, but that it is also at times illegally possessed, served and consumed in almost every sort of place where human beings foregather in the large cities of this country, with the exception. possibly, of religious edifices, courtrooms, cemeteries, schoolrooms, prisons, reformatories and W.C.T.U. headquarters.
The paragraph continues:
A well-known Detroit manufacturer in a public letter recently reviewed conditions existing under our prohibition laws. One paragraph from his letter is quoted herewith:
"Let's be frank. You and I know that there are enough common people in our great state who are breaking or condoning the breaking of the prohibition laws to possibly fill all the prisons of our whole country. You and I know that the people are going to have and use

Export Act-Mr. Robinson

alcoholic beverages. We know they are being made or used probably in every city block in our great city, and upon almost every farm in the country. And prohibition has been in force about ten years.
These views are merely typical of those expressed by unbiased observers in this country who, with courage and without hypocrisy, are willing to face the facts."
The following is an article which appeared in the Mail and Empire of January 1, 1930:
On the contrary, the chief critic has been Senator William E. Borah of Idaho, a Republican, who was one of the principal supporters of the prohibition plank of President Hoover's platform during the last presidential election in the republic. In a speech delivered on Christmas eve, Senator Borah asserted that the organization in charge of the enforcement of the Volstead Act, as at present constituted, would never enforce the law effectively. Since then he has charged that the administration of the permit system, under which alcohol is sold for industrial and scientific uses, "is a scandal," and that "practically open saloons are running in the jurisdiction of district attorney after district attorney.
The article continues:
"The root cause of the corruption which has dogged the prohibition unit from the beginning" is discussed, for example, in an editorial in the Baltimore Evening Sun. "Educated and intelligent men know," says this newspaper, "that high-grade men won't do low-grade work. They know that men of decency won't sniff around their neighbours' houses, nor snoop and spy upon t' e rest of the community. Since decent men won't do such work, it follows that the indecent flock to it, and graft and corruption are the inevitable result."
Probably my sensibilities for the tender feeling of the United States are not so pronounced as those of the Prime Minister, but that may be because I have lived on the border too long. I know many one hundred per cent Americans for whom I have great admiration, but I cannot say I have the same admiration for the United States as a country or as a nation.
I am of the opinion that this bill is framed for the interest of the United States to the detriment of Canada, and it will cause great injury to Canadian industry and Canadian working men. I think it is borne out by what has been said by the labour unions, especially the unions of Quebec, that this action has been taken at the demand of Mr. Dafoe of the Winnipeg Free Press, Mr. Jaffray of the Toronto Globe and Mr. Atkinson of the Toronto Star, in order that the government may obtain the one hundred per cent support of those papers during the coming election.
It would be well for the government to consider what the enactment of this legislation will mean for this country should the measure go into effect. It would certainly affect a

number of industries in Canada, and industries in Ontario in the last five years were hit pretty hard by the present government, especially the subsidiary companies that supply the manufacturers of agricultural implements. The same thing is true in connection with the automobile industry. Conditions in the automobile industry, so far as the workingman is concerned, would not have been what they were last winter and the winter before if the tariff had not been tinkered with in 1926. I was very much surprised that the federal government of the United States did not ask the assistance of the state of New York and other states in the union to cooperate but they absolutely refused to have anything to do with the enforcement of the Volstead Act.
This measure, when it becomes law, is going to make it extremely difficult for the provinces to enforce their laws. In other words, it is going to send the traffic underground, to a certain extent, as it was before the provinces had what they call government control. An editorial in the Detroit Free Press of March 17 has this to say:
At the risk of seeming to look a gift horse in the mouth, we could have *wished that in moving the second reading of the bill Mr. Mackenzie King had not urged its enactment on the ground that war might ensue between the United States and Canada.
Apparently Mr. Mackenzie King, a personal abstainer and a friend of amicable relations with this country, seized the first opportunity to introduce legislation as agreeable to a large element in Canada as to himself, which did not endanger his party's tenure of office. The effect of the measure will be the same, whatever his reason for delaying its introduction; but it would have come more gracefully if it had not been ushered in by reflections upon the law enforcement efforts of previous administrations in Washington, which seem to have been as fruitful, if not so noisy, as the efforts now being made.
The financial section of the Toronto Saturday Night, under date of March 15, has this to say:
Neighbourliness is all very well, but this stoppage of liquor exports to the United States is going to cost Canadians a pile of money (apparently somewhere between thirty to forty million dollars a year), and it is doubtful, to say the least, if the people of the United States really want them stopped. If they did. they surely wouldn't permit their anti-liquor law to be so flagrantly and universally flouted as it is to-day.
There have been several authenticated cases of prohibition agents on the Detroit and Niagara rivers losing their jobs because they took them too seriously. "Don't be too fussy about stopping 'rummies.' All you have to do is burn up gas and then stand by each month for your pay," was the instruction given one new patrol boat commander, as reported by him in a recent magazine article. The United

Export Act-Mr. Speakman
States should give some evidence of the sincerity of its desire to abolish the liquor traffic before Canada does herself the injury involved in putting the proposed law into effect.
The Toledo Times, on account of the war scare over this bill, has worked out how this military and naval warfare will be carried on. It will be interesting to the house to listen to this. It says:
The fleet conducting the blockade will number more than fifty ships, and the extent of the cordon and its field of operations will be highly remindful of a state of war between Canada and the United States, though such a condition is farthest from the minds of both. But nevertheless the American forces will be there. The old treaty providing for the limitation of armaments on the lakes may go hang. A celebrated German authority once described a treaty as a "scrap of paper," and we are adopting that view.
So now the only question as to how successful this law enforcing performance may become relates to the old problem as to how far we may persuade Canada to cooperate with us. If Canada will be real good, the united efforts of the two nations will undoubtedly make the undertaking a howling success.
Therefore we suggest that Canada should be solicited to duplicate our fleet of more than fifty vessels in lake Erie or anywhere else, according to the extent of our plans. Canada should provide a second cordon of "mother ships" with schools of small speed boats playing between, all equipped with devices inimical to the rum runner and munitions able to blow him out of the water.
Of course, the American blockade will be within the American boundary line, at least theoreticallv. and the Canadians should likewise shinny on their own side. But the boundary is merely an imaginary contraption, nothing to separate fleets on both sides of it by any material distance. Indeed, the two blockades may be located near enough, to one another to enable the crews of the "mother" and other ships to shake hands across the depths of water or to engage in other more convivial exchanges and repartee if they are so disposed.
It is an old philosophy that "one good turn deserves another." Therefore no doubt when we establish our proposed military border force of 10,000 armed men along the whole Canadian border, to enforce prohibition, Canada will again oblige us by doing likewise. Thus the world, may witness the heretofore unarmed border line of 3.000 miles armed to the teeth by land and water and by the naval and military forces of both nations.
It is a glorious picture. Fervently it is to be hoped that Canada will perceive her great opportunity to thus exemplify the spirit of peace on earth by granting us full cooperation in our laudable efforts to enforce our own laws. And if any unfortunate incidents ensue threatening to discontinue that peace with reference to the international border, there can be no doubt that both nations will fight valiantly, reviving the most heroic traditions of the Battle of Lake Erie.
I understand from what was said this afternoon that after this bill becomes law, we' are to make a treaty. If such be the case, I think it would be well to incorporate in that 2419-57$
treaty a provision that Canadians be treated like human beings in connection with deportation proceedings. I will give just two illustrations. A man was a life-saver at one of the bathing beaches at Windsor. A friend of his from Sandwich desired to cash a cheque in a Detroit bank and this life-saver just took out his rowboat and rowed his friend across the river. As he was about to let him off, the immigration officers arrested him while landing on the other side and they put him in jail. Prominent men of the golf club at Sandwich, the mayor of Windsor and other leading citizens gave the man a splendid character and asked that he be released, but the United States authorities would not release him, their excuse being that they were going to investigate. Those investigations take from one to five months and the man had to stay in jail.
Another man went to Arkansas, I think, to visit an uncle and he made up -his mind to live there. He married a Scotch girl and they had one child. Some fellow who wanted his job laid a complaint to the immigration officer, to the effect that the man was not legally in the country. This man, his wife and child were arrested and put in gaol. By the way he was bom in England and came to this country when he was about three years old. After a few days, they were let out of gaol but kept under guard for three or four months. He was not allowed to go to work or communicate with his family. They were shipped to New Orleans, then to New York, to be sent to England, where they did not know anybody. This man, his wife and child were sent to New York where the immigration authorities were persuaded to deport them to Canada. I contend, Mr. Chairman, that if Canadians were to treat Americans in that manner the people of the United States would feel like declaring war against us on the ground that we had committed an unfriendly act. But those are only two samples of what is going on all the time.

speechtext:
As one of those who
took advantage of the opportunity last year to express a fairly decided opinion upon this subject, I feel that it is incumbent upon me to say a word or two as to the principle of the bill before us and as to the action of the government. May I preface my remarks by congratulating the Prime Minister very highly. I wish to express my commendation of the real moral courage he has shown in bringing this bill forward at this time. In common, I suppose, with all members of the house I have been subjected during the last few months to an inundation of editorials and articles of one kind and other emanating I
Export Act-Mr. Speakman

know not whence, but I should imagine from one person or a small coterie of persons with a single mind, and all written with the object of impressing upon the reader the wrongiful-ness of this action by the government. The arguments were pretty well stereotyped. It was argued that it would cost Canada too much money, that we were attempting to assist the United States in enforcing a law which they themselves were not anxious to have enforced; and there were other arguments along the same line. The ifact remains that the government is at this time taking action which will result in one thing at least, and that is the clearing of the skirts of Canada, in clearing the character of Canada from the implication which whether brought forward by the United States or not, certainly was made by many Canadians, namely, that Canada was both conniving at and cooperating in this nefarious traffic. When I say nefarious traffic, I am not talking about the liquor business, although I might express myself in regard to that traffic in those terms; I aim speaking of the traffic of bootlegging and rumrunning liquor into the United States against the laws of that country. In vieiw of the rather discouraging, I will not say hostile, attitude in the house last year, and in view also of the inundation of literature of which I have just spoken, I think that the government and the Prime Minister in particular have shown great moral courage in taking this action.
There is one more thing I should like to say, and that is as to the reaction of the people of this country to this legislation. 1 had the opportunity of judging as to the reaction of a small section of Canada, because having taken the position I did, naturally I had many opinions expressed to me, and I found general approbation of the government's decision, and a very general desire on the part of the people in my part of the country that such action should be taken, and that Canada should cease to be a partner in that business.
Coming to the bill itself, the main exception that has been taken to it by those who have criticized the bill is that its implications far exceed the expressed intent of the government or the desires of this house and the country. The intent of the bill is very simple and, I think, wholly commendable. As I listened to the Prime Minister I judged that the full intent so far as the government was concerned was that the officials of the government should cease their active cooperation in this business, should cease to attach the signature of the government of Canada to 
the documents of rum-runners and bootleggers to enable them to convey their liquor illegally across the border. It is possible that the bill goes further than that. It states that under certain circumstances no intoxicating liquor shall be released or removed for the purposes of export to a country which has declared import of liquor illegal; in other words, that no liquor destined for export to such countries shall be released by the government officials from the warehouse in which it might be held. Had the bill stated that no liquor would be released when it was designated upon the manifest, permit or other proper document in the case that it was destined for export to the United States or some other country in a similar position, it would be satisfactory. I would like that to be made very clear, and the intent and implications of the bill made perfectly plain. While I am not a lawyer I have listened to the arguments brought forward by the legal gentlemen in this house, and it struck me that they might be correct. It strikes me that under the terms of this bill as expressed, not only would our officials be denied the right to sign the necessary permits or clearances, but it would place upon this country the definite responsibility of preventing such exports whether or not the United States or some other country in a similar position were designated on the permit. If that be the case, it would be going far beyond the intent of this house and far beyond the expressed intent of the Prime Minister in discussing this bill.
W'lth the purpose of the legislation as expressed by the Prime Minister I am wholly in sympathy. With the principle of the bill, which we have all endorsed, I am again wholly in sympathy, but I trust that the terms of the bill itself will make it very clear that it does not go beyond the refusal by our officials to connive at or cooperate in the export of liquor to a country that prohibits its importation, when it is stated on the manifest or permit that the liquor is desined for such country. That I understand is the real purpose of the legislation, and that purpose should be made perfectly plain. I, with other laymen in the house, am dependent on the law officers of the crown and upon gentlemen in the house with legal training. If the bill goes only to that extent, it will receive my hearty support. Naturally I would support the bill in any case. Not only am I committed to it; I heartily welcome it; but I would like to be very certain that we are not committing ourselves beyond the government's expressed intention, and committing ourselves to a course where we would find ourselves involved in greater complications

Export Act-Mr. Baldwin
than are possible at present, finding ourselves committed to enforcing the complete stoppage of export even when the country to which that liquor was to be exported was not designated in the documents. Upon these points I think the house deserves and should receive clear and definite information.

speechtext: Mr. Chainman, after listening to the hon. member for West Essex (Mr. Robinson) describe conditions in Windsor and Detroit I feel impelled to take part, in this discussion. I am pretty well acquainted with Detroit, I have a number of relatives there and this is the first time I have heard of such conditions as he speaks of. With regard to the Volstead Act, it is less than a year and a half since the electorate of the United States gave an overwhelming majority to the Republican party to carry out its .pledge to enforce prohibition. That was the chief plank in their platform. My observations are a little different from those of my hon. friend. If he will come down to the library he will find the Stanstead Journal which is published every week, and in its columns he will read that something more than one hundred automobiles engaged in smuggling liquor across into Vermont have been taken and probably half of the drivers arrested, sentenced and imprisoned. Many of those drivers are athletic men and when they see there is no chance of escaping with their automobiles they abandon them and run across country. We know that since the Volstead Act was passed about ten years ago, conditions have changed wonderfully in the United States. This is seen in the tremendous increase in the savings of the United States people, those savings having doubled, trebled and quadrupled in that time. Then look at the improvement in family conditions. Why, the wives and children now have a fair chance to live; they are better housed, better clothed, better fed, and better educated, and their family life is more wholesome. As regards arrests for drunkenness, under the Volstead Act there is not one arrest to-day where there were a hundred under the bid saloon conditions. Fifty years ago in New York clergymen from all over the world used to engage guides to take them through the Bowery, where it is estimated at least 100,000 people were living in the lowest depths of degradation. Is there any Bowery in New York now? Yes, the Bowery is there, but no longer does it harbour fallen humanity. Then take the condition of those who are socially inclined. People in the big cities want to have parties in their homes. Do they have liquor a.t those parties? No.

I come from a part of Canada where we believe in calling a spade a apade, and where such deplorable conditions as are described by the hon. member for West Essex do not obtain. I can tell the house that the captains of industry in the United States are a unit for the enforcement of the Volstead Act. I do not believe that any of us here will see the day when that act will be repealed, because the .people of the United States know what an untold blessing it has been to the poor people; it has enabled the poor man and his family to live respectably and well. As I have said, the whole time that I was in those great cities of the United States I did not see a single

person under the influence of liquor-a most remarkable situation. It has been said thait many of our men have been temipted to become bootleggers, but I can tell hon. members that so far as the Vermont border is concerned not one of our men who has left his legitimate work as a labourer, a farmer, or a mechanic and gone into that business but to-day is in rags and tatters-not one. Yet there was a time when it was said that this or that fellow had a fat bank account as a result of his bootlegging activities. But all those men have been dragged to jail, and they are, as I say, in rags and tatters and in disgrace. Every man of wealth in the United States who has financed this smuggling and bootlegging has become disgusted and glad of any opportunity to withdraw from it.
