Hon. JAMES MALCOLM (Acting Minister of National Defence) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Militia Pension Act to provide that pension may be granted to the widow of any officer who, at the time of his death being on full pay, dies after a period at which a pension might be granted to him, or who was at the time of his death in receipt of a pension.

Should we not have some
explanation of the meaning of this?

Militia Pension Act

When we get into committee I shall be glad to give that information.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the ohair.

This is a very minor
change in the Pension Act, but it is necessary to correct the anomalous position where an officer's widow is not provided for in case her husband dies in service even though under the act he may have been pensionable. There are two classes of pensioners under the Militia Pensions Act; one class of pensioner has to serve for twenty years; the other has to serve for ten years. Provision is made that when a man in receipt of a pension dies, his widow receives benefits amounting to about one-half of his pension. In the case of an officer who is pensionable after ten years' sendee, though he be twelve years in service, and although he would have been pensionable had he retired, if he dies in service, not having served the twenty years, his widow does not receive the pension. The matter has been .referred to the officers of the Justice department, who state that it is an anomaly in the drafting of the act. It is proposed to correct it in a bill by repealing subsection (14) of section 4 of chapter 133 of the revised statutes, and substituting the following:
Any officer who being seconded dies after a date at which a pension might be granted him shall if he is making the contribution hereinbefore required be deemed to be on full pay for the purposes of section 25 of this act.
That in brief is the purpose of the bill.
What has given rise to the amendment at this particular stage?

An anomaly has been created in the case of officers dying in the service after more than ten years' service. They would have been pensionable had they retired, but they died in service, and there is no way under the existing act to grant a pension to the widow.

Is there some case under
review at the moment of the widow of an officer who died in service and who would have been pensionable had he retired some years previously?

I cannot tell my hon.
friend whether any particular case has arisen or whether the officers of the department have simply discovered the anomaly, but I can get that information for my hon. friend.
I think we ought to have it. When was the section passed that is now being amended?

It is in the revised
statutes of 1927. I do not know when the original act was passed.
We had a revision of this act a year or two ago. I am not sure whether there were amendments to it last year or the year before, but certainly there have been amendments in the last couple of years.

I will give my hon.
friend all that information on the second reading.
We might as well give the minister notice now of what we want.
What provision is made for the widows of privates and non-commissioned officers?

The Militia Pension Act, which is copied very much after the English Act, makes no provision for contributions from subalterns and men. The officers make a contribution of five per cent, similar to the contributions made under the Civil Service Superannuation Act, but the men make no contribution, and no provision is made for the widows of the men. There is that difference between the two classes.
Does this act apply to the permanent force?
Yes.

Do the words "dies after a period at which a pension might be granted" mean that a pension may be granted upon voluntary retirement? Is a man granted a pension now if he retires of his own volition, or must he be retired to get the pension?

It is to cover the case of an officer who has served long enough to have been retired but who dies in the service. Under the act now his widow does not become a beneficiary. It is to correct that anomaly that this amendment is introduced.
I think the minister should be prepared to explain the last clause of the resolution. Does it apply to a particular case?
I shall be glad to get that information.
It says "or who was at the time of his death in receipt of a pension." Does that mean a war pension or a service pension?

A service pension. This has nothing to do with a war pension.
Militia Pension Act

The widow does
get a pension at the present time?
Yes.

It is difficult to
understand just what is meant by this resolution. We have been studying it to see what it means, but for the life of me I cannot understand it.

Perhaps I can explain
it better by saying this: There is one class which has been neglected under the act. If a man who is pensionable after ten years' service retires, he receives a pension, and if he dies his widow receives fifty per cent of that pension. But if the man who is pensionable after ten years, dies in the service, even after fifteen years' service, there is no provision in the act that his widow may receive any share of the pension. This amendment is to correct that anomaly.
It is not to cover any special case, but a general class.

A general class. The
act as it stands creates a hardship on the widow of the class of officer I have mentioned.
If the minister's explanation is correct, why are the words "or who was at the time of his death in receipt of a pension'' in this resolution?

I am going to ask my
hon. friends to let me introduce the bill tonight and furnish the information to-morrow. I could not answer my hon. friend's last question without seeing the officers of the department, but the general purport of the amendment I understand very well.

As the act is to
be amended, there is another anomaly which might be removed. An officer who has as much as ten years' service to his credit, and who has had deducted from his pay five per cent on account of pension, if he retires voluntarily receives no part of what he has contributed, as other civil servants do. The amount is simply confiscated. I do not think that is right. Upon retirement the amount to the credit of the officer should be returned to him, either with or without interest, as in the case of the civil servants who come under the Superannuation Act.
Is my hon. friend quite satisfied that the statement he is making is correct? I am not inclined to agree with him.

A case was called to my attention within the past few days of

an officer who had ten years' service to his credit and who retired seeing no future in the service.
A voluntary retirement?

Yes. I say that
in that case the amount to his credit on account of pension should be returned to him.

I want to differ with
my hon. friend. They are in exactly the same position as civil servants under the Superannuation Act. The man who has served under ten years, if he retires voluntarily, gets no return of his contributions. It is the same in both cases.

Having served ten
years, he gets nothing back if he retires voluntarily?
No.
He should.

The minister stated that there was no provision for deducting five per cent in case of the non-commissioned officers and men, that they did not come under this act. Is it not a fact that they desire to come under it and to get a pension, but that it has been refused?
No.

W ith all due respect for the minister, I think we should have some bettor explanation of this resolution. He has said quite clearly that this amendment will apply only in case the officer was in service at the time of his death, but the resolution says quite clearly, "or who was at the time of h:* death in receipt of a pension." I assume that 1 r W,aS *n receTt of a pension at the time of his death he could not be in active service and in receipt of full pay. It could not be both; I think I am right in that. This resolution says it is to provide a pension to the widow of any officer who at the time of his death is on full pay, or to provide her for a pension in case he was in receipt of a pension at the time of his death. That is not at all consistent with the minister's explanation, and if it is proposed to amend the act to provide for pensions to widows of officers who were in receipt of pension at the time of death, it is a very radical change. I am not opposing the change, it may be perfectly just; still, I think we ought to have a clear explanation of it.

I have an explanatory note which I have discovered among the papers

Militia Pension Act
sent to me by the officers of the department, and I think it will dispel my hon. friend's doubts if I read it. It is as follows:
The purpose of these amendments is to remove an anomalous situation respecting the provision for the widow of an officer who dies in the service, when such officer comes within that class of officers to which subsection (2) of section 4 of the Militia Pension Act relates, i.e.- those officers appointed to the force between the 1st of January, 1919, and the 31st of December, 1921, who are required to have ten years' continuous permanent force service in order to establish eligibility for pension, instead of a total of twenty years' service, as is required in the case of all other officers of the force.
Sections 25 and 27 of the act read as follow's:-
"25. Subject to the provisions hereinafter contained, the Governor in Council may, as to him seems fit, grant a pension to the widow and a compassionate allowance to each of the children of any officer who, having completed twenty years' service, was at the time of his death on full pay, or who, having completed ten years' service, was at the time of his death in receipt of a pension."
"27. The pension of a widow shall, if her husband was at the time of his death on full pay, be an amount equal to one-half of the pension to which he would have been entitled if he had been retired compulsorily immediately before his death, or, if at the time of his death he had been pensioned, an amount equal to one-half such pension."
It will be noted in the case of an officer who dies in the service that section 25 requires said officer to have completed twenty years pensionable service in order to enable a pension being granted to the widow. On the other hand, if an officer, coming within the ten year class, dies in the service after completing ten years' pensionable service, but less than twenty years' service, his widow is precluded from receiving a pension, though if he, in fact, had been retired with pension immediately prior to his death his widow would have been eligible to receive one-half of said pension.
In the case of an officer who dies in the service before a period at which a pension might be granted him, subsection (3). of section 11 of the act provides that there may be paid to the widow a gratuity equal to the deductions made, pursuant to the act, from the officer's pay during his service.
If, however, an officer coming within the ten year class mentioned, dies after completing ten years' pensionable service, but less than twenty years' service, his widow is, as stated, precluded from receiving not only a pension but the gratuity- authorized by said subsection (3) of section 11, for the reason, that her husband died after a period at which a pension might have been granted him had he been retired immediately before his death, but with less than twenty years' pensionable service, which, under section 25, he is required to have had in order to enable the grant of a pension to his widow.
It will thus be noted that an anomalous situation exists, and the purpose of these amendments is to remove the same, so that in the case of any officer who dies in the service after a period at which a pension might be granted him, his widow w'ill be eligible for the grant of a pension equal to one-half of that
which might have been granted the officer had he been retired immediately prior to his death. The provisions of the act, relating to the grant of a gratuity to the widow of an officer who dies before the period at which a pension might be granted him, will remain unaltered.
The words underlined in the sections of the draft bill indicate the amendments to the present sections to which said amendments relate.
I think probably my hon. friend understands the memorandum submitted by the officers of the department.
When I read it maybe I will.
The minister stated a moment ago that there was a deduction of five per cent from the officers' pay. Is that sufficient to cover the pension or is there a contribution by the government to the fund?

No, it is not. The five per cent deduction from the officers' pay and an equal amount contributed by the government would carry the pension to the officers; but there are the subalterns and the men who make no contribution, and in that case the government has to pay all.
And it would be necessary to pay the widows.

Yes. So as it stands I am informed by the officers of the department that the Pension Act takes about two dollars from the treasury for every dollar contributed. The reason it takes more than the genera! civil service fund is that a great part of the staff make no contribution whatever; in other words, the common soldier pays nothing.
Are pensions given to the widows of private soldiers and subalterns?
No.
But to the officers' widows pensions are granted?
Yes, and they contribute towards them.
Why?

In the case of the officers a contribution is made; that is the difference between thte two classes. The officers pay five per cent of their salary as a contribution to the pension fund, and another five per cent is contributed by the government. In the case of the privates and subalterns the whole ten per cent is paid by the government.

If the subaltern wanted
to pay five per cent would he be denied?

I think any civil servant could have elected to come under the pension act.
Privilege-Mr. Boulanger
I wish the minister would let us have that statement to read. I do not know whether anybody understood it or not; I know I did not.
It will be in Hansard.
It is about as clear as many of the pension sections.
In view of the fact that this affords an opportunity of discussion which otherwise might not arise, and as the memorandum will be in Hansard-
The bill will be printed.
The bill will follow the usual technical drafting.

The memorandum that
I have read is printed as an explanatory note to the bill.
That does not afford the same opportunity for discussion.
